name: non_turn_request
summary: The request is not a turn: not a turn path, or not a turn-shaped method on one.
trigger: The request path is not a known provider chat-completion endpoint, or the method on such a path is present and not POST.
grounding: Providers put non-conversation endpoints on the same host as conversation ones — token counting, model listing — and their successful responses contain counts and catalogues, not assistant content. Reducing those into turns would put non-conversation in the conversation log. The same argument covers method: a health probe against the chat endpoint is a probe, whatever path it names. This is a pure function of the request line, so every implementation can apply it identically, and one that does not captures a different set of turns from identical traffic.

examples.description: the Codex responses turn, on its own prefix
a gateway-prefixed turn path still resolves
a query string does not change the endpoint
a trailing slash does not change the endpoint
an absent method is not evidence of a non-turn method
a HEAD health probe on the turn path is a probe, not a turn
a GET on the turn path carries no turn to capture
token counting is adjacent to the turn path and is not conversation
an unrelated path on the same host

notes: `eligible` means the turn passes THIS gate, not that it is captured: a later gate may still refuse it. The HEAD example is the whole of the health-probe policy. There is no rewrite of a probe anywhere on this path — a probe is dropped under this reason like any other non-turn method, and nothing about the request or the response is altered. Both implementations apply this gate, against the same predicate over the same input: the path as the PROVIDER sees it. That is what the gateway-prefix example is about — a capture path in front of a route prefix must resolve the endpoint through it, not refuse the turn for the prefix. The gateway adapter is handed that path by its proxy; the standalone client computes it when it builds the upstream URL, because the path a harness emits can be a suffix of the provider's (a plan-authenticated Codex asks for `/responses` against a backend whose own base ends in `/codex`).
